identity_notes: Flaxseed has a very large legitimate human evidence base (87 kept of 159 screened), dominated by short-to-medium RCTs and many overlapping meta-analyses on lipids, blood pressure, and inflammatory markers, plus a smaller safety literature (anaphylaxis, gynecomastia). The largest lipid meta-analysis (31899314, 62 RCTs) and largest blood-pressure meta-analysis (36622248, 33 trials) both find modest but statistically significant benefits, concentrated in WHOLE flaxseed rather than flaxseed oil or isolated lignan extract -- form matters materially for this identity, and several records were flagged related_form_differs where an isolated lignan/peptide fraction or a fixed multi-ingredient product was tested instead of whole seed/meal. The inflammatory-biomarker literature is the most contested: an earlier widely-cited meta-analysis (31115436) was the subject of two published critical comments alleging analysis errors and undisclosed methods (32929447, 35100618, both with abstract text unavailable in this scope but titles alone are a material integrity flag); a larger, more recent GRADE-assessed meta-analysis (38971216, 54 RCTs, 2024) supersedes it and finds a smaller but still significant CRP/IL-6 reduction, no effect on TNF-alpha. Menopausal-symptom trials are mixed to null (20007337 null at low lignan dose; 22925074 inconclusive; 39364521 positive at higher dose). A pediatric bipolar-disorder RCT (20402707) and a young-healthy-adult flaxseed-vs-olive-oil RCT (23347535) were both null on their primary endpoints. Two case reports flag real safety signals: IgE-mediated anaphylaxis to linseed (12573209) and phytoestrogen-linked gynecomastia in a man (33303502). Many records were rejected as animal/plant-agronomy studies (flax crop genetics, cadmium/salicylic acid soil stress, animal feeding trials in rats/mice/pigs/dogs/poultry/cattle) that share the 'flax'/'Linum' keyword but are irrelevant to a human dietary supplement; several others were rejected because 'flax' referred to a woven bassinet (wahakura) or because the omega-3/ALA source was not confirmed to be flaxseed specifically.
